A runner travels 100 m east and then 100 m west to the starting point. Give the distance traveled and the displacement.
The total distance traveled is 200 m.
The displacement is zero.
The runner covers two hundred metres altogether but finishes with no net change in position.
The distance is zero and the displacement is 200 m east.
A walker completes a 60 m out-and-back trip in 30 s, ending where they started. Give the average speed and the average velocity.
The average speed is 2 m/s.
The average velocity is zero.
Sixty metres in thirty seconds gives a speed average of two metres per second, while the net-displacement rate is zero.
Both averages are 2 m/s forward because distance and displacement are identical.
An object moves around a circle at constant speed. State whether its velocity changes and the direction of its acceleration.
Its velocity changes because its direction changes.
Its acceleration points toward the centre of the circle.
The changing direction makes the velocity vary even at fixed speed, and the acceleration is inward.
Its velocity is constant and its acceleration points outward.
Velocity is a constant 4 m/s for 3 s. Find displacement and explain which feature of the velocity-time graph represents it.
The displacement is 12 m.
Displacement is represented by the signed area under the velocity-time graph.
The object moves twelve metres; this is the rectangular area beneath the velocity graph.
The displacement is 4/3 m and is found from the graph's slope.
On a position-time graph, what does the graph's height at a time represent, and what does its slope represent?
The graph's height gives position at that time.
The graph's slope gives velocity.
The vertical coordinate tells where the object is, while the steepness tells its rate of position change.
Height gives acceleration and slope gives total distance traveled.
A crate moves in a straight line at constant nonzero velocity while being pulled across a floor. State its net force and compare the pull with opposing friction.
The net force on the crate is zero.
The forward pull and backward friction have equal magnitudes.
The forces sum to nothing because the pulling force exactly matches friction in size.
The net force is necessarily forward, and the pull must be larger than friction.
A person pushes a wall. Identify the reaction force and say whether the action and reaction act on the same object.
The wall exerts an opposite force on the person.
The two forces act on different objects.
The wall pushes back on the person, with one force acting on the wall and its partner acting on the person.
The reaction is the person's weight, and both forces act on the wall.
An astronaut travels to a planet with half Earth's gravitational field strength. Compare the astronaut's mass and weight with their Earth values.
The astronaut's mass stays the same.
The astronaut's weight becomes half its Earth value.
The amount of mass is unchanged, but the gravitational force on the astronaut is halved.
Mass is halved while weight stays the same.
A powered car wheel rolls without slipping as the car accelerates forward. State the direction of the road's friction on that driven wheel and the slipping tendency it opposes.
The road's friction on the driven wheel acts forward.
It opposes the contact surface's tendency to slip backward relative to the road.
The road pushes the driven tyre forward because its powered contact patch tends to slide backward.
Friction on the wheel acts backward and assists the contact patch in slipping backward.
A falling object reaches terminal velocity in air. Compare drag with weight and state the object's acceleration then.
Upward drag equals downward weight in magnitude.
The object's acceleration is zero at terminal velocity.
Air resistance balances gravity, leaving no acceleration once terminal speed is reached.
Drag vanishes and the object continues accelerating downward at g.
A ball is launched horizontally. Ignoring air resistance, describe its horizontal velocity and its vertical acceleration.
The horizontal velocity remains constant.
The vertical acceleration is downward with magnitude g.
Its sideways speed stays unchanged while gravity accelerates it downward.
Its horizontal velocity steadily increases, and its vertical acceleration is zero.
Two stops produce the same change in momentum. One lasts twice as long. Compare their impulses and their average force magnitudes.
The two impulses are equal.
The longer stop has half the average force magnitude.
Both stops deliver the same momentum change, but spreading it over twice the time halves the mean force.
The longer stop has twice the impulse and twice the average force.
A 1 kg cart moving at 2 m/s sticks to a stationary 1 kg cart. Ignoring external impulse, find their shared velocity and state the conserved quantity.
Their shared velocity is 1 m/s in the original moving cart's direction.
The total momentum of the two-cart system is conserved.
They move together at one metre per second in the initial direction because the system's momentum is unchanged.
They move at 2 m/s because total kinetic energy must be conserved in a sticking collision.
For an isolated perfectly inelastic collision, state what happens to total momentum and to total kinetic energy.
Total momentum is conserved.
Total kinetic energy is not conserved and some is converted into other forms.
The system retains its momentum, but some motion energy becomes deformation or internal energy.
Momentum disappears while kinetic energy is always unchanged.
A force acts perpendicular to an object's displacement. State the work done by this force and explain using the force component along the displacement.
The work done by the force is zero.
The force has no component along the displacement.
It does no work because none of the force points in the direction of travel.
It does maximum positive work because all of the force acts along the displacement.
Two motors lift the same load through the same height. One takes half as long. Compare the useful energy transferred and the average useful power.
Both motors transfer the same useful energy to the load.
The faster motor has twice the average useful power.
The lift requires the same energy in either case, but completing it in half the time doubles the useful power.
The faster motor transfers half the useful energy and has the same useful power.
A ball falls from rest with negligible air resistance. Describe the changes in gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy.
The ball's gravitational potential energy decreases.
The ball's kinetic energy increases.
As the ball descends it loses gravitational energy and gains motion energy.
Its gravitational potential energy increases while its kinetic energy decreases.
Friction brings a sliding block to rest. Describe the main energy conversion and state whether total energy is destroyed.
The block's kinetic energy is converted mainly into internal or thermal energy of the block and surroundings.
Total energy is conserved rather than destroyed.
Motion energy becomes heating in the block and floor; the energy still exists in changed forms.
The kinetic energy turns into new massless energy, and the total energy is destroyed.
A 10 N force acts perpendicular to a lever 0.2 m from its pivot. Find the torque magnitude and say what happens if the same perpendicular force is applied at 0.4 m.
The original torque magnitude is 2 N m.
Doubling the perpendicular lever arm doubles the torque.
The first turning effect is two newton-metres; moving the same force twice as far from the pivot makes it twice as large.
The original torque is 50 N m and a longer lever arm halves the torque.
State the two independent balance conditions for a rigid body to remain in static equilibrium.
The net force on the body must be zero.
The net torque on the body must be zero.
All forces must balance and all turning effects must balance as well.
Only the upward forces must be zero, and a nonzero net torque is required.
The same force is spread over twice the contact area. State the new pressure relative to the old pressure and the formula used.
The pressure is halved.
Pressure is force divided by contact area.
There is half as much pressure because pressure equals the applied force per unit area.
Pressure doubles because pressure equals force multiplied by area.
In one stationary liquid of uniform density, compare the gauge pressures at depths h and 2h. State the relationship to depth.
The gauge pressure at 2h is twice that at h.
Gauge pressure in this situation is proportional to depth through rho g h.
Doubling the depth doubles the pressure above atmospheric pressure because the hydrostatic term is density times g times depth.
The deeper gauge pressure is half as large because pressure is inversely proportional to depth.
State what determines the buoyant force on an immersed object and the force condition for floating at rest.
The buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid.
For floating at rest, buoyant force equals the object's weight.
Upthrust matches the displaced liquid's weight, and a stationary floating object has upthrust balancing its own weight.
Buoyancy equals the object's volume regardless of fluid, and a resting float needs upthrust greater than its weight.
A sealed hollow metal object can float even though the metal itself is denser than water. Explain the effect of trapped air on average density and the density comparison associated with floating.
The trapped air increases volume with little added mass, reducing the object's average density.
A floating sealed object's average density is lower than that of the liquid when it floats partly submerged.
The hollow space adds size much more than mass, making the whole object's mean density low enough to sit partly above the water.
Trapped air makes average density larger, and partly submerged objects must have average density greater than the liquid.
A cup and a large tank of the same liquid are at the same temperature. What does equal temperature say about particle motion, and must their total thermal energies be equal?
At equal temperature, the particles have the same average thermal kinetic energy under the stated same-liquid conditions.
Their total thermal energies need not be equal because they contain different amounts of liquid.
The particles have comparable average motion energy, but the much larger amount of liquid can contain more thermal energy overall.
The tank's particles must move faster, and equal temperature guarantees equal total thermal energy.
A pure solid melts at constant pressure while heat is supplied and its temperature stays constant. State what the energy changes and whether average particle kinetic energy rises during the plateau.
The supplied energy changes particle arrangement and intermolecular potential energy during melting.
Average particle kinetic energy does not increase during the constant-temperature plateau.
The heat is used to change the material's structure rather than raise average motion energy while the temperature remains fixed.
All the heat raises average particle kinetic energy, and the particle arrangement remains unchanged.
Identify the heat-transfer mechanism in sunlight reaching Earth and in bulk circulation of warm water in a pan.
Sunlight transfers energy to Earth by radiation.
Bulk circulation of warm water transfers energy by convection.
Solar energy crosses space as electromagnetic radiation, whereas moving water carries heat by convection.
Sunlight arrives by conduction through empty space, and moving warm water is an example only of radiation.
A typical metal rod expands when heated. Describe the change in atomic motion and in average atomic spacing.
The atoms vibrate more energetically when heated.
Their average separation increases, causing the rod to expand.
Heating strengthens atomic vibrations and increases the mean spacing between atoms, lengthening the rod.
The atoms stop moving and pack closer together, making the rod expand.
Use the convention delta U = Q - W, where W is work done by the system. If Q = 100 J and W = 30 J, find delta U and interpret positive W.
The internal-energy change is an increase of 70 J.
Positive W denotes energy transferred out of the system as work.
Internal energy rises by seventy joules, while the positive thirty joules of work represents energy the system gives to its surroundings.
Internal energy increases by 130 J because positive W means work is done on the system.
A transverse wave travels along a rope. Distinguish the direction of wave propagation from the local rope particle's oscillation direction.
The wave disturbance propagates along the rope.
The rope particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
The pattern moves down the rope while each small piece moves across, rather than along, that direction.
The disturbance remains fixed and rope particles travel permanently along the rope with it.
For waves traveling at fixed speed, frequency doubles. State what happens to wavelength and the relationship connecting the quantities.
The wavelength is halved.
Wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength.
The spacing between wave crests becomes half as large because speed is frequency times wavelength.
Wavelength doubles because wave speed equals frequency divided by wavelength.
Explain why ordinary sound cannot cross a vacuum and identify what carries a sound disturbance through air.
A vacuum lacks the material particles required for ordinary sound propagation.
In air, interacting particles transmit pressure and density disturbances.
Empty space provides no medium for sound, while collisions and interactions in air pass on compressions and rarefactions.
Sound needs no material medium and travels through air only as visible light.
Compare particle motion relative to propagation in longitudinal and transverse waves.
Longitudinal-wave particles oscillate parallel to propagation.
Transverse-wave particles oscillate perpendicular to propagation.
The motion is along the travel direction for longitudinal waves and across it for transverse waves.
Longitudinal motion is perpendicular to travel and transverse motion is parallel.
Two pulses on a rope overlap. State what happens when their displacements have the same sign and when equal displacements have opposite signs.
Same-sign displacements add to produce a larger displacement.
Equal opposite displacements cancel at the overlap.
Pulses pointing the same way reinforce one another; equally large pulses pointing opposite ways give zero net displacement there.
Same-sign pulses cancel and equal opposite pulses always double the displacement.
A light ray meets a plane mirror at 30 degrees to the normal. Give the reflected angle to the normal and the angle to the mirror surface.
The reflected ray is at 30 degrees to the normal.
The reflected ray is at 60 degrees to the mirror surface.
Reflection leaves the ray thirty degrees from the normal, which is sixty degrees from the surface itself.
The reflected ray is sixty degrees from the normal and thirty degrees from the surface.
Light enters glass from air at an oblique angle. State what happens to its speed and the usual bending direction relative to the normal.
Its speed decreases on entering the glass.
It bends toward the normal.
The ray slows down in glass and turns closer to the line perpendicular to the boundary.
It speeds up and bends away from the normal.
Distinguish a real optical image from a virtual image by ray convergence and direct projection onto a screen.
A real image forms where rays actually converge and can be directly projected onto a screen there.
A virtual image is located by backward extensions of rays and cannot be directly projected onto a screen at that apparent location.
Real images form where rays actually meet and can be projected directly onto a screen; virtual images lie where backward ray extensions meet and cannot be projected directly onto a screen there.
Virtual images are formed by actual converging rays and real images are only backward extensions that cannot reach a screen.
State the refractive-index condition and the incident-angle condition for total internal reflection at a boundary.
Light must travel from a higher refractive index toward a lower refractive index.
The angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle.
The light approaches a less optically dense medium from a denser one and strikes above the critical angle.
Light must enter a higher-index medium, and any angle below the critical angle produces total internal reflection.
Define electric current in terms of charge and potential difference in terms of energy.
Electric current is the rate of charge flow.
Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge.
Current counts charge passing each second, whereas voltage counts energy transferred for each unit of charge.
Current is energy per charge, and potential difference is charge per second.
Two resistors are in one steady series circuit. Compare their currents and state whether resistors consume charge.
The same current passes through both resistors.
Charge is conserved and is not consumed in a resistor.
Both carry the same charge flow per second; resistors transfer energy rather than consuming charge.
The second resistor receives less current because charge is permanently used up by the first.
Two resistors connect between the same two nodes of a battery circuit. Compare their voltages and state the connection type.
Both resistors have the same potential difference across them.
They are connected in parallel.
The branches share one voltage because they form a parallel connection between the same pair of nodes.
Their voltages must be different because this is a series connection.
A resistor remains at 6 ohms while the applied voltage rises from 12 V to 18 V. Give the original and new currents.
The original current is 2 A.
The new current is 3 A.
Dividing voltage by six gives two amperes initially and three amperes afterward.
The current falls from 3 A to 2 A.
A tungsten filament becomes much hotter as its voltage increases. State the change in resistance and why current need not be proportional to voltage.
The filament's resistance increases as it heats.
The changing resistance means a constant proportionality between current and voltage cannot be assumed.
The hot wire resists current more strongly, so raising voltage also changes the resistance and the current-voltage ratio is not fixed.
Its resistance necessarily falls, so current and voltage must remain strictly proportional.
A device uses 100 W for 20 s. Give its energy use and explain what the power value means.
The device uses 2000 J of energy.
A power of 100 W means energy is transferred at 100 J per second.
It transfers two thousand joules altogether, at a rate of one hundred joules each second.
It uses 5 J, and 100 W means 100 coulombs are stored.
A charged rod attracts a neutral conducting object without touching it. Describe charge redistribution and whether the object must acquire net charge.
Charges in the conductor redistribute so opposite charge is nearer the rod.
Attraction by redistribution does not require the object to acquire net charge.
The conductor polarizes with unlike charge on the near side, while its total charge can remain zero.
All charges move equally far from the rod, and attraction proves the object has acquired net charge.
A charged particle moves parallel to a uniform magnetic field. Give the magnetic force and state the velocity condition needed for a nonzero magnetic force.
The magnetic force is zero for motion parallel to the field.
A nonzero force requires a velocity component perpendicular to the field.
Parallel motion experiences no magnetic push; a sideways component relative to the field is needed for one.
The parallel motion gives maximum force, and a perpendicular velocity component always removes the force.
Explain the condition for electromagnetic induction in a coil and state what happens when magnetic flux through a stationary coil is constant.
A changing magnetic flux through the coil induces a voltage.
Constant magnetic flux through the stationary coil produces no induced voltage.
The flux must change to generate an emf; with an unchanging flux in a fixed coil, no emf is induced.
A constant flux is required for induction, and a stationary coil always has induced voltage in any magnetic field.
Distinguish radioactive activity from half-life by stating what each measures.
Activity measures the number of nuclear decays per unit time.
Half-life is the time for the number of undecayed nuclei in a large sample to fall to half on average.
Activity is a decay rate, whereas half-life describes how long a large population takes to reduce by a factor of two.
Activity is the age of each nucleus, and half-life is the time at which every nucleus decays.
A radioactive isotope has a half-life of one hour. State whether one nucleus must decay after exactly one hour and what can be predicted for a large sample.
The decay time of a particular nucleus is random rather than fixed at one hour.
About half the initially undecayed nuclei in a large sample are expected to remain after one hour.
No individual nucleus has a scheduled one-hour decay; the statistical expectation is that half of a large sample survives that interval.
Every nucleus decays exactly at the one-hour mark, leaving none in a large sample.
In alpha decay, a nucleus emits a particle with mass number 4 and atomic number 2. State the changes to the parent nucleus's mass number and atomic number.
The daughter nucleus's mass number is lower by 4.
The daughter nucleus's atomic number is lower by 2.
The remaining nucleus loses four from its nucleon count and two from its proton count.
The daughter gains 4 in mass number and gains 2 in atomic number.
